title: Podcast: We Spoke to an Amazon Worker Destroying Books for AI
content:
We start this week with Emanuel’s follow-up to his Amazon book scanning story, in which he spoke to someone who worked in the Amazon warehouse which destroys books to train Amazon’s AI products. After the break, Emanuel and Sam tell us about the same few names appearing in LLM output over and over again. In the subscribers-only section, Joseph tells us why ICE is buying loads of data about ‘voter fraud’.

report.summary: An Amazon worker details how books are destroyed to train AI, exposing troubling data sourcing and copyright practices.
report.background: The report follows 404 Media's earlier investigation into Amazon's book scanning operations. A warehouse worker confirms that physical books are systematically destroyed after their contents are digitized for training Amazon's AI systems. This sheds light on the immense appetite AI companies have for high-quality text, especially as openly available web data becomes increasingly exhausted. Copyrighted books are considered valuable training material for their coherent language and factual density, but acquiring them typically involves licensing. Amazon's alleged use of scanned books without clear rights, and the physical destruction involved, raises serious ethical and legal questions. It also demonstrates how the race for AI dominance can drive companies to extreme lengths, often with hidden environmental and labor consequences.
key_points: A follow-up to 404 Media's Amazon book scanning story features testimony from a warehouse worker who describes books being destroyed to support Amazon's AI products. This confirms reports that physical books are being processed at scale, turning cultural artifacts into training data without observers typically seeing the resulting waste.

AI companies are likely using copyrighted books to overcome a shortage of public-domain or licensed training material. Destroying the books after scanning makes the practice easier to hide and harder to challenge legally, raising concerns about intellectual property theft and the preservation of knowledge, especially for rare or out-of-print works.

The same podcast highlights that large language models frequently generate the same few names across unrelated outputs. This repetition is a symptom of memorization and biased overrepresentation in training data, which can hurt AI creativity, spread stereotypes, and produce misleading results in real-world applications.

A subscribers-only segment reports that ICE is purchasing large amounts of data tied to 'voter fraud,' according to Joseph. This points to a growing commercial market for personal and political behavioral data, with AI-enabled analytics being applied to surveillance and enforcement—raising civil liberties issues far beyond AI training itself.

The episode ties together three threads: corporate AI's aggressive acquisition of data, the questionable quality and fairness of model outputs, and government use of data broker systems. Together they argue for stronger transparency, provenance standards, and regulatory oversight in the AI supply chain.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this exposes the ugly underbelly of data acquisition: even major firms may resort to destroying physical media to obtain training material. Developers could face legal risks and reputational harm if they unknowingly build on pirated or improperly sourced data. This may hasten the adoption of data provenance tools and more rigorous compliance. For ordinary users, the issue means models may regurgitate copyrighted text without authorization, and the hidden costs of AI—waste, environmental damage, and labor exploitation—will continue to grow. The ICE data story further highlights how AI systems are increasingly intertwined with surveillance and political monitoring, shaping who gets scrutinized and why.
report.tools: For readers exploring ethical data sourcing, watch Common Crawl for openly archived web data, EleutherAI's The Pile for transparent multi-source text, and Hugging Face Datasets for metadata provenance and filtering. Tools like the Open Data Institute's data ethics canvas and dataset inspection libraries such as Great Expectations are useful for auditing corpora. For research into AI memorization and repeated names, see ‘Data Portraits’ from the University of Washington and related model auditing toolkits like AI Fairness 360.
